title: Three of Each, Gently Falling
statement: Consider sequences $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_9$ of integers in which each of the integers $1$, $2$ and $3$ appears exactly three times, and no other integer appears. How many such sequences satisfy $a_k \le a_{k+1} + 1$ for every integer $k$ with $1 \le k \le 8$?
hints: Since every term is $1$, $2$ or $3$, list the adjacent pairs $(a_k, a_{k+1})$ that break $a_k \le a_{k+1} + 1$.

The only forbidden pair is a $3$ immediately followed by a $1$. Delete the three $3$'s. The six remaining terms can be arranged in any way. Then ask where blocks of $3$'s can be put back. This is a stars and bars count.

Each maximal block of consecutive $3$'s must be immediately followed by a $2$ or end the sequence. So the $3$'s are shared among four slots: just before each of the three $2$'s, or at the end. Count the arrangements of $1,1,1,2,2,2$ and the ways to share three identical $3$'s among four slots, then multiply.
solution:
For values in $\{1,2,3\}$ the inequality $a_k \le a_{k+1}+1$ fails only when $a_k = 3$ and $a_{k+1} = 1$. So we count arrangements of $1,1,1,2,2,2,3,3,3$ in which no $3$ is immediately followed by a $1$.

Delete the $3$'s. This leaves an arrangement $w$ of $1,1,1,2,2,2$, and there are $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ such arrangements. In the full sequence, each maximal block of $3$'s is followed either by nothing or by a $2$ or $1$ of $w$. The forbidden case is a $1$. So the blocks of $3$'s occupy some of four slots: immediately before one of the three $2$'s of $w$, or at the end.

Conversely, take any $w$ and distribute three $3$'s among these four slots. Every $3$ is then followed by a $3$, a $2$ or nothing, so the result is valid. Distinct distributions give distinct sequences. By stars and bars there are $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ distributions.

Hence the number of sequences is $20 \cdot 20 = 400$.
